# Embodied Land

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-07* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/07/embodied-land/)[^original-post]

I recently wrote, in **[Scattergood and the Hub](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/scattergood-and-the-hub)**, about **“what did not reach us.”***What did not reach us* is one of the five arcs that form the throughlines of my life that began from what I learned at Scattergood Friends School. We learned about communities of integrity, personal integrity and Quaker practice.

*What did not reach us* is about what we did NOT learn, i.e. about Quakers as settler-colonists, and our role in the Indian Boarding Schools.

![](https://i0.wp.com/channelsintoknowledge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image.png)

#### Embodied Land

It surprised me that research I’ve done revealed **“Embodied Land”** as another of the throughlines of my life experiences.

The reason I can understand that concept now is because of what I’ve learned from my Native friends over the past decade. I’ve learned how integral their relationship to the land is to Indigenous peoples. This is also something that *did not reach us.*

The land has been important to me in many ways throughout my life, but I hadn’t put those experiences together as relationships with the land.

Both things were true at the same time. My relationship with the land was real. **The ignorance was also real.**

#### My Land Experiences

I have had a deep, genuine, lifelong embodied relationship to land and simultaneously, I was almost completely ignorant of what Indigenous peoples’ relationships to those same lands looked like, meant, or required.

I grew up on farms in central Iowa. Scattergood’s name has been changed to Scattergood Friends School and Farm, one indication of the importance of the farm to the school. Not only does significant food for the school come from the farm, but the farm is also used in many ways as an educational tool. When I attended Scattergood in the late 1960s, the sophomore biology class focused on each of us raising pigs. Farm crew was one of our work crews. We also worked in the orchard.

Some of my deepest spiritual experiences occurred when our family camped in the Rocky Mountains. It was a nightmare image of my beloved mountains hidden behind clouds of pollution that triggered my decision to live without a car. That meant that the time I would have spent driving was time I was connected to the land instead. Either by walking, running or riding a bicycle. When I was keeping a log, I was running about 1,100 miles a year.

Not having a car meant that I usually walked to and from work. My photography is almost always about the natural world, and improved significantly when I began to carry my camera with me during these daily walks. I typically take around seventy photos a day.

#### Marches

It is ironic that marches I was involved with, the 1969 Peace March from the school to Iowa City, the 2013 Climate March from the school to Iowa City, and others were meaningful to me. But I now know I missed these opportunities to intentionally build my relationship to the land.

#### First Nation-Farmer Climate Unity March

This changed for me as I walked the 94 miles along the path of the Dakota Access Pipeline over eight days in 2018. The intention of the march was for a small group of Native and non Native people to spend this extended time together sharing stories and learning about each other. I began to learn about Indigenous relationships with the land as I talked with and observed the ways the Native people shared with us during those long walks down empty Iowa gravel roads.

They pointed out the standing water in the fields that didn’t drain because the topsoil was not preserved when the pipeline’s trench was filled. Instead a mix of soil and clay was used, the clay interfering with the drainage of the fields.

They pointed out various plants growing along the road.

But it was when we would stop each time we actually walked over the pipeline that I began to know the land.**I could feel the evil below us.** We gathered together, held hands, many were brought to tears.

[![](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21uI53%21%2Cw_1456%2Cc_limit%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe5e81d40-79b6-46fc-82a2-a7eb30728331_2000x1333.jpeg)](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21uI53%21%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe5e81d40-79b6-46fc-82a2-a7eb30728331_2000x1333.jpeg?ssl=1)

#### Now that I know and am still learning

I am now part of the planning committee for the Decolonial Repair Network, created by Sikowis and Eric Anglada to support GPAS and the work of Indigenous-led repair. That work has brought me to the Great Plains Action Society’s Urban Resilience Hub in Iowa City — a little over an acre of land, newly in Indigenous hands, being transformed into a healing sanctuary, mutual aid garden, and community gathering space.

I have spent work weeks there: digging, moving soil, doing what needed doing under Indigenous direction. I was not there to lead or advise. I was there because the land asked for work, and I was part of the community doing it.

# How Knowledge Travels

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-08* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/08/how-knowledge-travels/)[^original-post]

Working through the throughlines of my life, I found one I hadn’t expected: *What Did Not Reach Us.* That is a statement, not a question.

In naming this path, I considered several possibilities. Some framed it as an intentional cover-up of the Quaker history of settler-colonialism. But that isn’t what happened at Scattergood Friends School, where I graduated in 1970. Our teachers, I believe, knew little about this history or its consequences themselves. At the time there was little public awareness of the tragedies of forced assimilation of Native children. Indigenous communities and historians were well aware. Quakers, however, did not then have the relationships with Native peoples that would have taught them these things.

There was a public awakening when what appear to be the remains of Native children began to be discovered on the grounds of those institutions of forced assimilation. That discovery deepened a growing awareness of the injustices of settler-colonialism that continues today.

*This is a story about people whose good intentions were shaped by assumptions they could not see, operating within a colonial system that presented them with only certain choices and certain ways of understanding what they were doing.*

As discussed below, knowledge can be thought of as water flowing through channels. Water doesn’t reach where there are no channels — not because the water isn’t there, but because the channel hasn’t been built. That is what ***what did not reach us*** means.

What is called for now is building the connections that weren’t there before. Engaging with the work of the Great Plains Action Society (GPAS) is one way to begin. Those connections go back to 2017, when Sikowis Nobiss — founder of the GPAS — spoke at the annual sessions of Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative) (IYM(C)) about building bridges with Native Americans. IYM(C) members have since participated in work weeks at the GPAS’s Urban Resilience and Innovation Hub in downtown Iowa City. Friends can also support this work by attending the monthly online meetings of the Decolonial Repair Network (DRN), which was created specifically as a way for allies to support GPAS. I help maintain the DRN website: ***<https://decolonialrepairnetwork.blog/>***

# My example of how it reached us

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-08* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/08/my-example-of-how-it-reached-us/)[^original-post]

I’ve asked, “[WHAT did not reach us?](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/what-did-not-reach-us-web-app)” And “[WHY did this history not reach us?](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/not-an-excuse)”

These questions refer to the Quaker involvement in the Indian residential schools in this country and Canada. Which were institutions of forced assimilation.

Those words do not reveal the horrible things that often happened there. That is a large part of **what did not reach us.**

What follows is a specific example. Two years ago I was blessed to be included in a ceremony related to the deaths of two Native children and their unmarked graves in West Branch, Iowa.

A remarkable series of events unfolded from a research paper by Park Ranger Peter Hoehnle, a National Park Service guide at the Herbert Hoover National Historic Site, who holds a doctorate in history. This is a link to that paper, [The West Branch Industrial School](https://bit.ly/4cMdgS5).

West Branch, Iowa, is just two miles west of where I attended high school, at Scattergood Friends School. But I never learned (Arapaho) Grace Yellowhair’s story. That she was buried in an unmarked grave in West Branch.

Her story didn’t reach me until 2024, when my friend Judy Cottingham, of the West Branch Quaker meeting, came across Peter’s paper and thought of me, knowing of my interest and concerns related to the Indian boarding schools. From there it traveled the way these things travel when people decide not to look away — Judy to me, me to my friend Paula Palmer, whose ministry is about Quakers and the residential schools.

Paula sent it on to Frank MedicineWater, the Cheyenne-Arapaho tribal officer working to identify the children who attended these schools and to trace their descendants. Frank carried it to Fred Mosqueda, the Arapaho Language and Culture Program Outreach Coordinator for the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes of Oklahoma. Fred wrote back that his wife had been raised by her grandfather, Gustave Yellowhair, and that he believed he could trace the line to Grace.

Judy kept up the correspondence with Fred, especially about his wish to come to the gravesite, and did the research to locate the two unmarked plots — Grace Yellowhair and Theodore Rogers, an Osage boy, buried near each other in the Friends’ section of the West Branch Municipal Cemetery. Before the gathering that Monday, city staff placed white flags to mark the spots.

[![](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21stMR%21%2Cw_1456%2Cc_limit%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbd8dd58c-782a-4198-a1db-3353f62424e4_6399x3006.jpeg)](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21stMR%21%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbd8dd58c-782a-4198-a1db-3353f62424e4_6399x3006.jpeg?ssl=1)

White flags identify unmarked graves of Grace and Theodore in the West Branch, Iowa, cemetery. Just two miles from where I had attended Scattergood Friends School.

The family did not want to disinter Grace’s remains. But they felt it necessary to come to the gravesite to perform the ceremonies that would allow Grace to pass over to the other side. Since that had not been done before, her spirit could not leave. With the ceremony, her spirit was finally set free.

Fred Mosqueda came from Oklahoma for the ceremony, with his wife, Mary Fletcher, and her brother, John Fletcher. It was not a public event. Those gathered at the grave that Monday, July 22, 2024, included Judy and Jim Cottingham, members of the West Branch Friends Meeting of Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative), Peter Hoehnle, members of the West Branch Friends Church, and the town’s mayor. I was there to witness, and to take the photographs the family had asked for.

As we waited, I watched Fred move slowly through the gathering, greeting each one of us. Then he began by telling us, from the inside, why children like Grace had been taken at all — how the Army had killed the buffalo so the people would be confined to the reservations, and how families had no choice but to give up their children or lose the food and supplies the government had promised them. It was a hard thing to hear this history spoken from an Indigenous perspective.

Cedar was burned, and feathers were used to fan the smoke. Fred sang three songs with the drum he had brought. These allowed Grace’s spirit, held in that ground for a hundred and forty-one years, to finally leave and cross to the other side. Theodore Rogers was remembered in the prayers, so that he too could go. We stood together in silence to witness it. I strongly felt the presence of the Spirit.

Afterward we shared a meal at the West Branch meetinghouse. That, too, was part of the ceremony — the last meal Grace would share with her family on earth. They made up a plate of food for her and set it outside, in a sheltered spot.

This is what I mean when I ask what did not reach us. It was not the phrase “forced assimilation” that failed to reach me; those words I had heard. What did not reach me was Grace — a fifteen-year-old Arapaho girl who died in a Quaker school and lay in an unmarked grave two miles from the school that formed me, for a hundred and forty-one years, and I never knew.

And I have come to see that it did not simply fail to reach me. It was kept and not looked at, not spoken of, for all those years. That is the harder truth inside “what did not reach us.” Not that the story lost its way to us, but that we did not go to it.

What other stories should we be looking for?

# My mistake

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-08* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/08/my-mistake/)[^original-post]

There is a danger, which you might already have noticed, that the phrase “what did not reach us” can be seen as absolving us from any more prayer or action related to the history of Quaker involvement in the Indian boarding schools. “What did not reach us” is passive. When in actuality, knowledge was **withheld** and harms were **done**.

I have been trying to find a mechanism to get Quakers to move past trigger words that result in shutting down any real discussion of the issues. Unfortunately, that probably worked **because** nothing more was being asked.

What is needed is to bridge **“what did not reach us”** to **“and therefore, this.”** Ask the hard, uncomfortable questions:

After we are moved by these stories, what are we being asked to relinquish?

* Is it land?
* Is it money?
* Is it our comfort?
* Is it the cherished story of our own moral goodness?

My friend Sikowis Nobiss, founder of the Great Plains Action Society, has said:

…She (Sikowis) has spoken to congregations — Mennonites, Quakers, Catholic Workers, and others — and in nearly every conversation, she says, she hears **‘a cocktail of white guilt combined with a desire to be in proximity to Indigenous folks’ that leads only to more inaction.** Giving land back, she reminds us, is the single most powerful thing settlers with inherited wealth can do — and almost none of those conversations have ever led to it.

After the First Nation-Farmer Climate Unity March that I walked on with Sikowis, she answered my question, “what can I do?”, with the assignment that shaped my years since: learn and teach LANDBACK. My teaching is in part done by writing blog posts like this. At the time Sikowis said that, I created the blog [***LANDBACK Friends***](https://landbackfriends.com/)

Subsequent blogs I created and have written on about these subjects are:

* [Quakers and Religious Socialism](https://quakersandreligioussocialism.com/)
* [Unflinching](https://unflinching.blog/)
* [Active Objection](https://activeobjection.substack.com/)

---

**Undo the Machinery of Not-Reaching**

I’ll continue to pray and write about these things. And I’ll do my best to fulfill what I am asked to do by the Spirit. I’ll continue to work with the Decolonial Repair Network, and the Great Plains Action Society. To show up when I can when invited to work at the GPAS’s Urban Resilience Hub.

# Not an excuse

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-08* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/08/not-an-excuse/)[^original-post]

I’ve been troubled by my observations related to **“what did not reach us.”**

I’ve come to see that phrase as a way in for Quakers to begin to get past the words that trigger many Friends to shut down any attempts to discuss settler-colonialism and its consequences. I believe that can be a valid approach to help Friends begin to address our current condition as people who continue to benefit from this colonialism. And by extension, as a people who continue this oppression of Indigenous peoples.

But there is the obvious question. **Why did this history not reach us?**

How did my ancestors, shaped by a testimony against violence, and by sacrifice for it, come to run schools that inflicted it — and then, for generations, not see that they had?

The answer comes from the very story that made Friends proud. That they were the humane alternative to the Army’s brutality and the corruption of the Indian agencies related to Native people. Those were the reasons President Grant cited when he engaged Quakers to become involved in the US government’s actions and policies related to Indigenous peoples, actually calling it his “Peace Policy”, sometimes referred to as “Quaker Policy”.

A narrative of benevolence is an unusually effective concealing device precisely because it is sincere.

Soldiers who kill know themselves to be killing.

Teachers, on the other hand, sincerely believed they were “helping” the Native children by teaching them how to adapt to the encroaching colonial culture. And they felt they could pass that belief, undisturbed, to their descendants.

To me.

# The Gap

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-08* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/08/the-gap/)[^original-post]

**What Did Not Reach Us** is one of my life’s throughlines.

That line is completely different from the other throughlines because it begins with **absence**. That **absence**was an awareness of how settler-colonists, which included Quakers, completely dispossessed Indigenous peoples of their lands and their culture with genocidal violence. **Absence**of awareness of the tragic history of forced assimilation of Native children.

**You don’t know what it is that you don’t know.**

The only way to begin to become aware of something you didn’t know is when that missing knowledge is revealed from relationships with **those who do** hold that knowledge.

I wasn’t aware of this throughline until I began to get to know Native people. And from them I slowly began to learn what I had not known, **what did not reach us**.

When I graduated from Scattergood Friends School in 1970, I felt I had received a good education about **Quaker practice** and personal integrity. I learned about **community integrity**at Scattergood, because community meetings and work crews taught us how to be in community by actually living that way. I learned about **personal integrity** from observing the lives of our teachers and Quakers of my meeting, and studying the lives of Quakers throughout history. I learned critical thinking skills and how to become a life-long learner.

It was that Scattergood education that helped me understand the profoundly adverse consequences of fossil fuels and the car culture. I was led to not have a car during my adult life.

It was that Quaker education that made me pay attention when I was in the presence of Native people who came to our public gatherings to stop building fossil fuel pipelines. But there wasn’t time to begin to build relationships with any of them.

It was that Scattergood education that made me pay attention when I began to hear about the Quaker involvement in the Indian boarding schools. And when I heard Sikowis Nobiss speak about building bridges with Native peoples at Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative) in 2017.

I was discovering the gap in what did not reach us at Scattergood back then. The gap included teaching nothing about settler-colonialism or Quaker involvement in the Indian Boarding Schools. About who had lived on this land before Scattergood was built. About the lives of Native people in today’s world.

But paying attention is not the same as understanding. And understanding is not the same as knowing what you do not know.

#### How I began to discover *what did not reach us*

[As I previously wrote](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/how-knowledge-travels), knowledge can be thought of as water flowing through channels. Water doesn’t reach where there are no channels — not because the water isn’t there, but because the channel hasn’t been built.

In 2018 I was blessed to be able to begin to create a channel to the knowledge I had not known that I did not know, a channel to Indigenous peoples and their ways. That was when I participated in the ***[First Nation-Farmer Climate Unity March](https://firstnationfarmer.com/)***, that was organized by Sikowis Nobiss and Ed Fallon. The intention of that march was to create the conditions for a small group (about 30) of Native and non-Native people to be together for an extended period of time (8 days and nights) to share stories and begin to understand each other across our cultural gaps.

One of the things that usually happens when you begin to gain new knowledge is that it changes you. I was profoundly changed by what I began to know during those long walks down empty Iowa gravel roads, along the black snake of the Dakota Access Pipeline. I gained insights into the Native people and their lives. And they began to teach me that the land is our relative.

[![](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21iygV%21%2Cw_1456%2Cc_limit%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd7d697c9-e468-4d7a-b818-25f2ba930514_3305x3023.jpeg)](https://firstnationfarmer.com/)

**[Matthew and I on the First Nation-Farmer Climate Unity March (2018)](https://firstnationfarmer.com/)**

I received the first shock to my system early in the march from a story one of my new Native friends told me as we walked together. The reason we were on this subject was because I told him I knew of the Quaker involvement in forced assimilation, and that I was very sorry that had happened. He just nodded and we continued to walk together. But several hours later he came to me, and told me he had a story to tell. The story had just recently happened. One day his mother called him, very upset. She had seen a story from Standing Rock that immediately took her back to the childhood stories she had heard related to taking children to the residential schools.

[Note: my decision to bring up the subject of the boarding schools was not something I took lightly.]

That experience was the beginning of a channel to Indigenous knowledge. You cannot learn that from a class or book. That is what did not reach us at Scattergood. But this is how knowledge began to travel through that channel to me (and I hope some of my knowledge might flow in the other direction).

That channel has led me to the work being done at the Great Plains Action Society’s Indigenous-led Urban Resilience Hub in Iowa City. Knowledge continues to flow through the channel. Authentic relationships continue to evolve there.

* Community of integrity

# Why Tell the Story of the March?

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-08* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/08/why-tell-the-story-of-the-march/)[^original-post]

My new awareness of how knowledge is transferred has me wondering if I should be writing more about the First Nation-Farmer Climate Unity March. Knowledge cannot be transferred from reading text.

But, the March is an example of how knowledge begins to be transferred. It was designed for this very purpose, to provide the extended time required for a channel to begin to open between Native and non-native people. For the critical relationships to develop.

But you cannot walk ninety-four miles with Native and non-native people. This is the paradox. “Why write about something no one can replicate?”

### What a story can do

#### Open a door

A story can reveal something that you were not aware of that you did not know. It cannot transfer knowledge about that, though.

For that, you need an **evolving connection** with those who have that knowledge. Evolving meaning building a deepening relationship over time with the knowledge keepers.

#### Carry desire, not data

Stories make people want the encounter that changes them. **Desire is portable**; experience is not.

#### Transmit the pattern

The content can’t be copied, but the method can. **Find your local silence**, show up in your body, and let the story follow. Because it will.

When someone hears these stories and feels the pull to see for themselves, the first impulse is usually the wrong one — to arrange a visit, to go and look, to treat the work and the people as something to be toured. That impulse is not a fault; it is simply the only model of learning most of us were ever given.

But the March replaced that question with a better one, and it is the question I want to leave you with:

*Not* ***“may I see it?”*** *but* ***“what is being asked of me, now that I know?”***

# Grammar of Silence

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-09* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/09/grammar-of-silence/)[^original-post]

An accurate historical analysis requires a grammatical **conversion**: from the passive voice of **“what did not reach us”** to the restored agency of “**what was actively withheld**.”

I am beginning to see why I had no idea of the real impact of settler-colonialism on the Native people of this land — including the role of my own faith community, Quakers. The **passive**language by which settlers thought and spoke about the people they overran is not an accident of style. It is the finished product of **withholding**, the**grammar the silence** was designed to produce.

An example: “Iowa was opened to settlement.” Converted: “The United States forced the Sauk, Meskwaki, and Ioway from Iowa through coerced treaties, and sold their land to settlers — including the families whose farms I grew up among. **The land is held under that taking today**.”

Notice what the conversion requires: an **agent**(the United States), a **mechanism**(coerced treaties), the **present tense** (the land is still held), and the **speaker**(me, in the sentence). The withholding had the same parts. Quakers operated Indian boarding schools; curricula taught the silence; my own meeting did not assign the reading. And the knowledge never went missing for Native people — they carried it, at great cost, all along. It was withheld from settlers, by settler institutions, some of which I belong to.

The language we choose will not finish the work, but it determines where the work can begin. A sentence with no agent asks nothing of anyone. A converted sentence ends with someone holding something — and what is held can be returned.

It is up to us to decide what language we will use, and that choice will determine whether we move forward in our understanding, or instead remain trapped in ignorance.

Being able to convert from “**what did not reach us**” to “**what was actively withheld**” is a practice you can learn.

This interactive web app I created will help you practice how to do this. ***<https://kislingjeff-oss.github.io/ConversionFromPassiveToActive/>***

It includes an exercise for converting your own passive sentence into an active sentence. This is one of my examples:

# Knowledge withheld versus missing

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-09* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/09/knowledge-withheld-versus-missing/)[^original-post]

It is crucial to differentiate between knowledge that is ***missing***versus knowledge that was ***withheld***.

Knowledge that is ***missing***is found by study and research. Teachers in classrooms provide knowledge to students. Prior to taking the class, the students likely didn’t have much knowledge of human anatomy, for example. That knowledge was missing prior to the class. And that knowledge was found via teaching and study during the class.

Knowledge that is ***withheld*** cannot be taught in a class. You cannot study your way across a withholding. A withholding is not a gap in the information — it is a break in a relationship. The only thing that repairs a broken relationship is to restore one by building a channel.

One piece of knowledge that had been withheld from me was the role Quakers played in the Indian boarding schools. Quaker involvement in the Underground Railroad is a story Quakers like to tell. But I didn’t hear stories about what happened during the forced assimilation of Native children. **The story stayed on the other side of a boundary I had never crossed — I had no relationship with the Native people who carried that memory, and no channel by which it could reach me.**

Knowledge that has been withheld cannot travel on its own. It can only travel through relationship. A relationship strong enough to carry knowledge across a boundary is what I call a channel — and without knowing the word, I have been building channels all my life.

I’ll be writing a lot about building channels in subsequent articles.

# Nightmare arrives 50 years later

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-09* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/09/nightmare-arrives-50-years-later/)[^original-post]

This photo of mine led me to live without a car in Indianapolis for my entire adult life there. It is a photo of Long’s Peak, with Moraine Park in the foreground, in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado. # ‘Then I lost my spirit’

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-09* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/09/then-i-lost-my-spirit/)[^original-post]

![](https://i0.wp.com/channelsintoknowledge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-5.png)

*Historical view of White’s Indiana Manual Labor Institute. Source: WTHR*

I’m about to begin to re-tell the story of the First Nation-Farmer Climate Unity March. I originally wrote the story as it was happening, writing blog posts each evening that we walked during the eight days and ninety-four miles of the March, and then numerous articles about it since. The original website holding those writings and photos is: [**First Nation Farmer Climate Unity March**](https://firstnationfarmer.com/).

I’ll be re-writing those stories from the perspective of eight years later, and about what I have learned since the March. The March was where I began to understand “what did not reach me… because it was withheld.” Where my channel to Native ways of being in the world began to form. Where knowledge was transferred.

***I had read what I could find about forced assimilation prior to the March, but the knowledge did not transfer to me until someone I was beginning to know shared his personal story with me on an empty gravel road in Iowa.***

I plan to continue to explore “What am I called to do now?”

Much of this relates to the significant, ongoing, intergenerational trauma of what were called Indian boarding schools. Nothing like the schools most of us who are not Native attended.

No, these were institutions of forced assimilation of Native children, where all kinds of trauma occurred.

It is important to hear the voices of the Native people affected by this. That is why I’m sharing the story Zitkála-Šá wrote about her boarding school experiences with you now.

---

#### Zitkála-Šá

Zitkála-Šá (translated as “Red Bird” from the Dakota language, and also known by her missionary-given name, Gertrude Simmons Bonnin) became an influential Yankton Dakota writer, editor, translator, musician, and political activist.

She was born in 1876 on the Yankton Indian Reservation in South Dakota. At age 8, she went to White’s Indiana Manual Labor Institute, a Quaker Indian boarding school in Wabash, Indiana. **She later attended Earlham College, a Quaker school in Richmond, Indiana. The same college I attended.**

Her story, [*“The School Days of an Indian Girl,”*](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/10376/pg10376-images.html)was published in The Atlantic Monthly, February 1900, about her experiences at White’s Institute. She eloquently describes the horrors that happened to her there. She wrote, **“Then I lost my spirit.”**

---

##### THE CUTTING OF MY LONG HAIR.

The first day in the land of apples was a bitter-cold one; for the snow still covered the ground, and the trees were bare. A large bell rang for breakfast, its loud metallic voice crashing through the belfry overhead and into our sensitive ears. The annoying clatter of shoes on bare floors gave us no peace. The constant clash of harsh noises, with an undercurrent of many voices murmuring an unknown tongue, made a bedlam within which I was securely tied. And though my spirit tore itself in struggling for its lost freedom, all was useless.

A paleface woman, with white hair, came up after us. We were placed in a line of girls who were marching into the dining room. These were Indian girls, in stiff shoes and closely clinging dresses. The small girls wore sleeved aprons and shingled hair. As I walked noiselessly in my soft moccasins, I felt like sinking to the floor, for my blanket had been stripped from my shoulders. I looked hard at the Indian girls, who seemed not to care that they were even more immodestly dressed than I, in their tightly fitting clothes. While we marched in, the boys entered at an opposite door. I watched for the three young braves who came in our party. I spied them in the rear ranks, looking as uncomfortable as I felt. A small bell was tapped, and each of the pupils drew a chair from under the table. Supposing this act meant they were to be seated, I pulled out mine and at once slipped into it from one side. But when I turned my head, I saw that I was the only one seated, and all the rest at our table remained standing. Just as I began to rise, looking shyly around to see how chairs were to be used, a second bell was sounded. All were seated at last, and I had to crawl back into my chair again. I heard a man’s voice at one end of the hall, and I looked around to see him. But all the others hung their heads over their plates. As I glanced at the long chain of tables, I caught the eyes of a paleface woman upon me. Immediately I dropped my eyes, wondering why I was so keenly watched by the strange woman. The man ceased his mutterings, and then a third bell was tapped. Every one picked up his knife and fork and began eating. I began crying instead, for by this time I was afraid to venture anything more.

But this eating by formula was not the hardest trial in that first day. Late in the morning, my friend Judéwin gave me a terrible warning. Judéwin knew a few words of English; and she had overheard the paleface woman talk about cutting our long, heavy hair. Our mothers had taught us that only unskilled warriors who were captured had their hair shingled by the enemy. Among our people, short hair was worn by mourners, and shingled hair by cowards!

We discussed our fate some moments, and when Judéwin said, “We have to submit, because they are strong,” I rebelled.

“No, I will not submit! I will struggle first!” I answered.

I watched my chance, and when no one noticed, I disappeared. I crept up the stairs as quietly as I could in my squeaking shoes,—my moccasins had been exchanged for shoes. Along the hall I passed, without knowing whither I was going. Turning aside to an open door, I found a large room with three white beds in it. The windows were covered with dark green curtains, which made the room very dim. Thankful that no one was there, I directed my steps toward the corner farthest from the door. On my hands and knees I crawled under the bed, and cuddled myself in the dark corner.

From my hiding place I peered out, shuddering with fear whenever I heard footsteps near by. Though in the hall loud voices were calling my name, and I knew that even Judéwin was searching for me, I did not open my mouth to answer. Then the steps were quickened and the voices became excited. The sounds came nearer and nearer. Women and girls entered the room. I held my breath and watched them open closet doors and peep behind large trunks. Some one threw up the curtains, and the room was filled with sudden light. What caused them to stoop and look under the bed I do not know. I remember being dragged out, though I resisted by kicking and scratching wildly. In spite of myself, I was carried downstairs and tied fast in a chair.

I cried aloud, shaking my head all the while until I felt the cold blades of the scissors against my neck, and heard them gnaw off one of my thick braids. Then I lost my spirit. Since the day I was taken from my mother I had suffered extreme indignities. People had stared at me. I had been tossed about in the air like a wooden puppet. And now my long hair was shingled like a coward’s! In my anguish I moaned for my mother, but no one came to comfort me. Not a soul reasoned quietly with me, as my own mother used to do; for now I was only one of many little animals driven by a herder.

[*Zitkála-Šá, “The School Days of an Indian Girl,”*](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/10376/pg10376-images.html) *The Atlantic Monthly, February 1900, collected in* American Indian Stories *(1921), public domain via Project Gutenberg (#10376). Background on White’s Manual Labor Institute from the U.S. National Park Service and the American Friends Service Committee.*

# Clarifying who “we” are

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-11* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/11/clarifying-who-we-are/)[^original-post]

This article comes from the vague feeling of unease I sometimes get when I use the pronoun “***we***”. One of those things I should have paid more attention to.

“***We***” means different things in different contexts, and by not being clear about which meaning I am implying, real confusion can occur. And there is the danger that by not being clear, someone can feel they aren’t included in the “***we***” I’m writing about, and thus feel they have no obligations related to the subject at hand.

A list of eleven different ways “**we**” can be used is included at the end of this. Three more are marked as missing from the list: Native Friends, family, and those who supported without going.

It surprised me to see how many ways “***we***” can be used. In my writing from now on, I intend to be clear about which meaning of “***we***” I’m referring to.

**[I created this interactive web app](https://kislingjeff-oss.github.io/WhichWe/)**that allows you to explore different ways that “***we***” can be used.

[![](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%2103R8%21%2Cw_1456%2Cc_limit%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5c2c5e20-2616-4dae-9492-25719c375c37_651x762.png)](https://kislingjeff-oss.github.io/WhichWe/)

**<https://kislingjeff-oss.github.io/WhichWe/>**

---

#### **Distinct Pronouns**

##### Note: ‘**Your**’ refers to you, the reader. And some of the specifics are related to Quakers.

**1. We who operated the schools.** Quakers, institutionally, 1860s–1900s. Not metaphor: named people, named schools, federal arrangements. *This “we” is yours by inheritance and cannot be declined.*

**2. We who were taught the benevolent story.** Quakers of your generation, told our relatives went to help. *Not culpable for the schools; fully accountable for what we do now that we know.*

**3. We who were not reached at Scattergood — students and teachers together.** The most delicate of them, and the most generous. Your teachers belong in this “we” with you, not on the other side of it.

**4. We who are Friends today.** Iowa Yearly Meeting Conservative, Bear Creek, every meeting that owns property. *The “we” that can actually be asked for something.*

**5. We settlers.** Everyone living on this land who is not Indigenous. Broadest, least useful for obligation, necessary for accuracy.

**6. We who knew the science.** Environmentalists, climate-aware people, you from the beginning of the discussion. *A “we” defined by having understood and been unable to act.*

**7. We who walked.** The roughly thirty Native and non-Native people, September 1–8, 2018. Yours to use — *we walked together* — because you were there.

**8. “We are a tribe.”** Donnielle Wanatee’s sentence on the fourth day. *Hers. Receivable, never assumable, never a membership card.*

**9. We of the coalition.** These are some of the coalitions I’ve been involved with: the Buffalo Rebellion, fossil fuel pipeline work, and Des Moines Mutual Aid. *A working “we” of Native and non-Native people with a task, which is the only kind that has ever produced anything in my story.*

**10. We of the Hub.** People who show up to the work weeks under Indigenous direction. *Includes me and does not confer authorship.*

**11. We facing collapse.** All of us, and the only place the pronoun is honestly universal — with the immediate qualification that the collapse arrived for Native peoples in the nineteenth century.

# Doing your own research

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-11* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/11/doing-your-own-research/)[^original-post]

Recent writing here has been about Quaker records, and about our relationships with the Native peoples of this land — or the lack of them. That is the point of this series: to get you to look into your own records. Arriving informed is a form of respect, and every question you can answer with your own research is a question you don’t spend on a relationship. There is a saying in oppressed communities that “it is not our job to educate you.”

#### Your own research

Yesterday’s post named four things a record can be: RECORDED, LEFT OUT, NEVER OPENED, or OPENED AT LAST. The classification matters because it tells you what kind of work is in front of you. A record that was left out calls for you to research what is missing. A record nobody opened calls only for someone to open it.

[![](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21FtMR%21%2Cw_1456%2Cc_limit%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F44f8757e-560e-4ba6-bf7d-59ea60c245cc_1086x550.png)](https://kislingjeff-oss.github.io/SortingTheRecord/)

#### [Interactive](https://kislingjeff-oss.github.io/SortingTheRecord/)

It takes some practice to sort real documents this way, so I wrote an interactive to practice on. Nine actual records, and you decide what each one is: [Sorting the Record](https://kislingjeff-oss.github.io/SortingTheRecord/)

[![](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21alRu%21%2Cw_1456%2Cc_limit%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb10c6d1a-0c3e-4bb1-88eb-bffae5f3fd7f_1074x635.png)](https://kislingjeff-oss.github.io/SortingTheRecord/)

---

#### What is missing?

One goal of this research is to find what was **LEFT OUT** — the disease, the deaths, the objections and the grief that the ledgers do not mention. You find those by reading what is there against what is missing.

Of course you need some records in the first place to practice this classification. What has been **RECORDED**might need to be uncovered. At my Quaker meeting many historical documents were in a safe in the meetinghouse. But for many years we could not access those documents because we couldn’t unlock the safe. Recently, the safe was unlocked, revealing a treasure trove of documents. These documents could be considered **NEVER OPENED** (in recent times).

Part of the impetus to get the safe open was so we could discover the past history of the relationships among Friends and Native peoples.

The papers in that safe have been waiting a long time. This is a chance to make them **OPENED AT LAST**.

---

*To the clerk of \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_Friends Meeting,*

*I am writing to ask three questions about our own records.*

*1. Where are this meeting’s historical records held, and who is responsible for them?*

*2. Which of them have been cataloged, and which have never been read? I am asking particularly about any material touching Indian boarding schools, Indian affairs committees, or schools operated by Friends.*

*3. If any of it has never been read, may I read it, and may I report what I find to this meeting?*

---

**NOTE**: For Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative) Friends, many of our yearly meeting’s documents are in the Iowa State Historical Society’s archives. There is some concern about the recent decision to close the Iowa City archives and send them to Des Moines. There is ongoing litigation to try to prevent that.

**They open one at a time, and the key is silence.** After you read a letter you will be asked to sit with it for two minutes, in the Quaker manner. Ten letters is twenty minutes of silence. If that sounds long, that is the point, and it is the shortest honest version of it. There are no discussion questions. If a letter needs a worksheet it has failed.

# Reasons why knowledge fails to reach us

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-11* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/11/reasons-why-knowledge-fails-to-reach-us/)[^original-post]

I have been shocked not just at what I continue to learn about Friends’ involvement in the forced assimilation of Native children, but it has also been heart wrenching to realize how much of this history Friends chose not to write down — and then chose not to read.

Harder still is seeing the intergenerational trauma that history produced, and its effects on my Native friends. I could not see any of that until I had a couple of channels into their lives. The trauma was there the whole time. The channels were not.

---

[![](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21FrOe%21%2Cw_1456%2Cc_limit%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9c4db31f-c0af-44fd-a8b7-caf74fbd5ec8_1202x461.png)](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21FrOe%21%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9c4db31f-c0af-44fd-a8b7-caf74fbd5ec8_1202x461.png?ssl=1)

---

There are three different things going on in our records, and they are worth keeping separate.

#### **Intent**

Lying means knowing. We don’t know what the clerk of Quaker meeting knew or intended in 1883, when Grace Yellowhair died at the West Branch Industrial School, for example.

#### **The records that mislead**

Quaker school records of that period documented attendance, crop yields, and student behavior. They left out disease, abuse, the children’s objections, and the grief of their families and their nations. They left out that two of the children died.

*(See below: 1883 — two Native children died and were buried in the West Branch cemetery, in unmarked graves.)*

The later official history does the same thing in a gentler tone: a paragraph about Friends going to the schools to help Native children.

*(See below: 1971–2023 — Left out. The official history is written.)*

#### **The records nobody read**

Thousands of pages sat in Friends’ archives for a century, unopened. Nobody lied there. There is no false impression, because there is no statement at all.

*(See below: 1884–1950 — Never opened.)*

#### Opened at last

One instance: Peter Hoehnle, a ranger at the Herbert Hoover National Historic Site in West Branch, wrote a paper about the West Branch Industrial School — from sources that had been available the whole time.

*(See below: 2024, the paper — Opened at last.)*

# The Choice

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-11* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/11/the-choice/)[^original-post]

I was recently led to make a difficult choice. My yearly meeting, Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative) just finished its annual sessions, where our work as Quakers during the past year was discussed and decisions were made about the ongoing work of the yearly meeting.

Many of the monthly meetings (local meetings that have business meetings every month, and meetings for worship every week) that belong to the yearly meeting have seen declining membership. In addition, the generation of Iowa Quakers I grew up with, who did much of the work of the yearly meeting during our lives, are now aging and dying.

[![](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21KHQK%21%2Cw_1456%2Cc_limit%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0e950164-3ee8-4a22-99a4-2d8a9071ea4c_2517x882.png)](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21KHQK%21%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0e950164-3ee8-4a22-99a4-2d8a9071ea4c_2517x882.png?ssl=1)

I, and I know others, feel a greater need to participate in the work of our monthly and yearly meetings, since there are fewer of us to do the work. In the past I served as clerk of the yearly meeting’s Peace and Social Concerns Committee, and of the Publication Committee. I was also on the Scattergood School Committee for several years.

#### The Conflict

The Great Plains Action Society held a marathon teach-in, [Truth and Liberation in Action](https://actionnetwork.org/events/truth-and-liberation-in-action-marathon-teach-in), last Saturday. The full schedule of the GPAS event is at the end of this post.

Unfortunately, that was also one of the days of the Quaker yearly meeting annual sessions. Thus the choice I was faced with.

I have known and worked with Sikowis Nobiss, founder and Executive Director of the Great Plains Action Society (GPAS), since 2017. We have been together on many occasions, including pipeline protests, and we both walked 94 miles along the path of the Dakota Access Pipeline during the First Nation-Farmer Climate Unity March in 2018. She has become a close friend of mine.

I am part of the planning group for the Decolonial Repair Network (DRN), which Sikowis had set up with Eric Anglada as a way for non-Native people to learn about colonization, to learn how to be good accomplices for Indigenous peoples, and to financially support the work of GPAS. I got connected to the DRN because Eric contacted me based upon Sikowis’ suggestion of people she knew who might be interested in joining. Several other Quakers from my yearly meeting attend the monthly Zoom meetings.

Last fall Sikowis had a dream that led GPAS to purchase — to re-acquire — an acre of land in downtown Iowa City, which was named the **Indigenous-led Urban Resilience and Innovation Hub**.

I feel blessed to have been able to join the four work-weeks that have been held at the Hub. The first was during the first week of December (2025) when we focused on gutting the interior of what will be the **Healing Justice House**. It was heavy, dirty work in sub-freezing temperatures, but so satisfying to see the results. Significant friendships were made as we did this work together.

That was followed by work-weeks in March, April and May (2026).

It was significant that the Quaker boarding high school I attended, Scattergood Friends School, offered meals and housing for anyone participating in the work-weeks. The school is just 15 miles from the Hub. I stayed at the school during each of the work-weeks. My Scattergood roommate from years ago, Jon Tesdell, who is also a member of my Quaker meeting, joined a couple of the work-weeks and stayed at the school as well, where we were roommates once again. We appreciated the opportunities to visit with the students and staff about our work at the Hub. During the first work-week I was grateful to speak about this work during an all-school community meeting (Middle and High School students).

#### Truth and Liberation in Action

I was led to attend the Truth and Liberation in Action Marathon Teach-In last Saturday. I tuned in to the Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative) annual sessions via Zoom whenever I could during the week, but I missed that entire day.

#### Why?

I spent quite a while sitting with this choice. The leading to attend the GPAS event was clear from the outset, but I was pretty sure that many Quakers would disagree. The most difficult decisions are those that will upset people you care about.

One of the fundamental principles of engaging with those suffering oppression is that what you learn comes with an **obligation for ongoing support**. An accomplice commits to the relationships being built. Which includes showing up for the work being done by the oppressed community, which you are becoming a part of.

#### Centering Indigenous leadership

This is part of the fundamental principle of **centering Indigenous leadership**. This has been one of the greatest barriers I’ve encountered as I try to get more Friends involved in working with Native people. That does NOT mean, as I have heard some Friends express, that we surrender our practices and beliefs regarding living Spirit-led lives.

My experience is this work has been enhanced by my Spiritual leadings. It has led me to live more faithfully. There is the dark history of Quaker involvement in what was done to Native peoples. My ongoing work with Indigenous peoples has helped me find ways to deal with some of that history, and its ongoing presence today.

#### The Hub is Working

I looked forward to seeing the spaces we have been building at the Hub put into action. It was sort of miraculous to see presentations during the Teach-In happening in what had been, six months ago, a dirty, abandoned building, now transformed into a meeting room with freshly painted walls.

![](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/%24s_%21AGnL%21%2Cw_720%2Cc_limit%2Cf_auto%2Cq_auto%3Agood%2Cfl_progressive%3Asteep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc73587bf-1980-490b-9432-19192098ffea_7008x3944.jpeg)![](https://i0.wp.com/channelsintoknowledge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-6.png)

A building transformed

It was also exciting to hear from so many diverse organizations that have been building relationships with GPAS and the Hub. **Hub**is the right word for what has been happening, and will continue to develop.

#### What happened?

*Note: I really don’t like calling attention to myself, but these are some of the things that **happened because I was there** at the Hub during the Teach-In.*

A Scattergood staff member attended and we talked about the Hub and the school. She told me students at the school were **inspired** by what was happening at the Hub, and that she was looking forward to “getting her hands dirty” by working at the Hub herself.

A **Mennonite**man who recently moved to Des Moines with his wife sought me out to talk about connections with our faith communities. We exchanged contact information.

Several different times during one of her presentations, Sikowis referred to work I’d been doing.

* She talked about the **volunteers**who came to help build the Hub. And pointed me out in the audience as one of those volunteers.
* She talked about the **Decolonial Repair Network (DRN)** and mentioned that I was part of the network. She gave me the opportunity to talk a little about that with the audience.
* She also spoke about my writing going deeply into the issues of colonialism, and asked me to tell the audience the link to my **blog**.
* And Sikowis mentioned all the **photos**I’ve taken at and for the Hub. I was taking photos during the Teach-In, too. <https://photos.app.goo.gl/dAn7fSZMdRUjqJkR7>

#### Interpretation

I’m glad I was led to attend the Teach-In. I had no idea ahead of time that all these wonderful things would happen. But I did anticipate good things would happen based upon previous experiences.

I feel it is important for me to continue to be faithful to leadings that often move in unanticipated directions. And faithful to my commitments to continue to support the Great Plains Action Society and the Hub. Important to continue to help center Indigenous leadership.

#### The Future?

I think work such as we are doing at the Hub can energize Quakers’ justice work. Scattergood students are inspired. Most of the volunteers at the Hub tend to be younger people with a deep drive to work for justice. Deep spirituality has been part of our work at the Hub. I believe this has the potential to attract more people to our Quaker meetings.

It is also important to note that this work requires changes in our traditional ways of working for justice. We (Quakers) need to learn how damaging some of our justice efforts in the past have been, so we don’t continue to repeat those mistakes.

We cannot just drop in at the Hub, expecting to be given a “tour.” We must recognize we are entering sacred spaces. And must listen before we speak.

We’ve been working on guidelines for visitors. Here is part of the current DRAFT of them.

---

#### DRAFT of part of the visitor guidelines being developed for the Hub

*You are welcome here. The Great Plains Action Society’s Resilience Hub was brought into being by Indigenous leadership for all people—as a place of healing, mutual aid, and community resilience. At the same time, this space carries a spirit and a history that asks something of you in return. These pages invite you into a way of being present that honors the land, the people, and the generations whose knowledge lives here.*

#### Whose Land You Are Standing On

*Iowa City occupies the homelands of Native American Nations to whom we owe our commitment and dedication. The area of Iowa City was within the homelands of the Iowa, Meskwaki, and Sauk and because history is complex and time goes far back beyond memory, we also acknowledge the ancient connections of many other Indigenous Peoples here.*

#### The Spirit of this Place

*The GPAS Resilience Hub at 810 Maiden Lane is not a museum or a cultural exhibit. It is a living, breathing center of Indigenous-led community life. The healing sanctuary, gathering spaces, event hall, and mutual aid garden here are consecrated by the intention and sacrifice of Indigenous people who have fought for generations to keep their cultures, their languages, and their peoples alive.*

***When you walk in, you are crossing a threshold. Not a door, but a way of being. Sacred spaces are not defined by walls—they are defined by the spirit poured into them and the responsibility accepted by all who enter.***

# What was withheld from us?

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-11* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/11/what-was-withheld-from-us/)[^original-post]

I’ve been working through the difference between **“what did not reach me”** and **“what was withheld.”** Some of this is specific to me, a seventy-five year old white male and a Quaker. Much of it generalizes to Quakers today.

It has taken me a while — both to do the research, and to work out why so many Friends still know so little about our own history with Native peoples in this land.

The two phrases are not the same claim. If something was withheld, the wrong belongs to whoever withheld it. You are the injured party, owed an apology and owed disclosure. “Withheld” excuses you.

“Did not reach me” does not. If it did not reach you, the obligation is yours: build the channel. I have been writing about how we build these channels, and I will keep writing about that.

**[This web application, Four Tracks](https://kislingjeff-oss.github.io/FourTracks/)**, sets out what did, and did not, reach me. The table reads the same years four ways:

* **What was done.** To children, by name where we have names.
* **What Friends recorded.** Our own minutes and official histories — and what they left out.
* **What was public.** In print, in newspapers, in national magazines, in federal files.
* **What reached me.**
  * The rows **before**my birth in 1951 are marked *not yet born*. There was no one there yet to reach.
  * From 1951 to 2011 — a Quaker childhood, four years at Scattergood, forty years of service in Indianapolis — every row is marked NONE OF THIS HISTORY REACHED ME.
  * Not until 2018, when Matthew Lone Bear told me about his mother and the residential schools, does that column read “**the channel opens.**” Only then did I have the beginnings of a channel to learn this history.

Two buttons at the top change what you see.

“**Show only what was public, and what reached me**” dims the other two columns, leaving the distance between those two as the only thing on the screen.

“**Show where our own record failed**” marks the places our own record broke down. Four places where our record left something out. Three where it was kept and never opened. Only one of those is something somebody did. The other, the original history is written, is something nobody did — harder to name, because there is no one to accuse. The result at my end was identical: the history did not arrive. Which is why “who withheld it” turns out to be the less useful question. **No one has to confess before a record can be opened.**

If the failure were **withholding**, you would need an admission from someone before anything could move. Because most of it is **abandonment**, a meeting can act this month without waiting for anyone to own up.

# Why is it necessary to study this at all?

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-18* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/18/why-is-it-necessary-to-study-this-at-all/)[^original-post]

“This” refers to the concepts and examples of building channels into knowledge. Specifically, knowledge that you cannot learn about and understand just by study. In my case, as a 75 year old white male Quaker, I could not understand racial injustice or Indigenous knowledge by studying, much as I had tried to do so.

Why didn’t I just support those communities financially and stay out of the way? Why not let those with the knowledge decide what to do with that support? Exploring this is the purpose of this new blog.

---

This table displays the three major grounds for doing this work ourselves.

![](https://i0.wp.com/channelsintoknowledge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-13.png)

## Religious

My (Quaker) religion has an intense focus on finding truth. But, some of my Quaker ancestors were involved in the institution of slavery, some actually having their own enslaved people. All the non-Native people in this country are the beneficiaries of the theft of Native lands. My Quaker ancestors, and relatives, were involved in the forced assimilation of Native children.

For our own spiritual integrity, we must develop these channels, because we cannot understand the truth about these things otherwise. Our search for truth is blocked until we do. Until we do, we will continue to make poor, or even harmful decisions. And we will not have a path to speak to our complicity in these injustices.

## Generational

I have only recently begun to realize how deep the silence of Quakers has been. This continued unfaithfulness. I don’t want oncoming Quakers to suffer this same silence. So that these Friends don’t continue the mistakes Quakers have made. And can’t see better ways until they become aware of how to build channels into Indigenous and racial knowledge.

## Survival

Our environmental catastrophe is unfolding at an alarming rate. Most non-Native people are dependent on external systems and services for our very survival. Systems that are collapsing. Traditional Ecological Knowledge is centuries old and has helped Indigenous people across the world to live in harmony with our environment. This is the very knowledge we, non-Native people, will need to learn if we are to survive.

# What is a channel?

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-24* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/24/what-is-a-channel/)[^original-post]

## A channel is

> A relationship strong enough to carry knowledge across a boundary is what I call a channel — and I realize that I have been building channels all my life.
> Jeff Kisling, *Knowledge withheld versus missing*, 14 July 2026

---

* **A relationship.** Not a resource, not a text, not a database, not an app. A channel is made of people who know each other.
* **Strong enough.** There is a threshold. Being in the same room does not clear it. Being on the same mailing list does not clear it. Something has to have been built, and the building is the part that costs.
* **To carry knowledge.** Not a friendship for its own sake. It is a conduit. Something travels.
* **Across a boundary.** Between cultures, between communities, between generations. Where there is no boundary you do not need a channel — you need a library.

## The image it comes from

---

> Knowledge can be thought of as water flowing through channels. Water doesn’t reach where there are no channels — not because the water isn’t there, but because the channel hasn’t been built. That is what ***what did not reach us*** means.
> Jeff Kisling, *How Knowledge Travels*, 27 June 2026
>
> ---

![](https://i0.wp.com/channelsintoknowledge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-17.png)

The picture separates existence from availability. The knowledge was always there and was carried at great cost. It did not go missing and it did not dry up — only the conduit was absent. That relocates the failure from persons to infrastructure, and it names the remedy: you do not summon water, you build channels.

Where the image breaks is the more interesting part. An irrigation ditch runs one way, downhill, and is unaltered by whatever passes through it. A channel between people runs both directions, and it changes both ends.

## Why a channel is needed at all

A reasonable person asks: if the history is real and the books exist, why not simply read the books? Because there is more than one kind of not-knowing, and only one of them is repaired by reading. Knowledge that is *missing* is found by study — nobody stands between you and it. Knowledge that is *withheld* is a different condition entirely.

---

> You cannot study your way across a withholding. A withholding is not a gap in the information — it is a break in a relationship.
> Jeff Kisling, *Knowledge withheld versus missing*, 14 July 2026

---

The only thing that repairs a broken relationship is to restore one. That is what a channel is for, and it is why the sequence below cannot be hurried.

What follows is the order in which it actually happens.

## The order things happen in

0 **A leading.** Something stirs in the one who does not yet know. It comes from outside the picture and it has no name yet.
1 **Two people, and a boundary between them.** One holds knowledge the other does not. It has been carried, at cost, all along.
2 **Something crosses.** A story, an invitation, an encounter. It reaches them and surrounds them.
3 **The Gap opens, and the building begins.** They now know what is missing. The stirring could not name it; the story that crossed can.
4 **The channel opens the rest of the way.** Invitation, presence, shared work and cost. Years of it, and the second half is slower than the first.
5 **And it runs both ways.** A one-way channel is extraction.

---

Click on image to start animation: <https://kislingjeff-oss.github.io/ChannelsIntoKnowledge>

[![](https://i0.wp.com/channelsintoknowledge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-22.png)](https://kislingjeff-oss.github.io/ChannelsIntoKnowledge)

## Three things to notice

* **Nothing is transferred when the story crosses.** The cloud that surrounds them is beautiful and useless. A story opens a door; it cannot carry what is on the far side of it.
* **Knowledge travels as soon as the channel is open, not once it is finished.** It moves along whatever has been opened so far, carrying as much as that will hold.
* **It has reached them only when the channel connects.** A channel that stops short has not arrived, however much is moving along it.

## How to read the colors

* Gold – The knowledge itself. It is in the first figure from the beginning, and it is the last thing to reach the second.
* Teal – Everything that is not the knowledge — the story that crosses, the channel, and the labor and support that travel back.
* Pale white – The leading. Its own color on purpose, so it cannot be mistaken for the knowledge arriving early.

# Defining statement revised

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-25* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/25/defining-statement-revised/)[^original-post]

This idea of creating channels into knowledge is evolving as I think and pray more about it.

My original statement was: *The only way for non-Native people to understand so they can respond to injustices that Native people endured, and continue to suffer from, is to create channels into that knowledge.*

On further reflection, there are some problems with that statement.

* Native people are depicted solely as those who have suffered, when actually they
  * hold the knowledge,
  * offer the invitation,
  * set the direction,
  * and lead
    * Ronnie James at Des Moines Mutual Aid
    * Sikowis Nobiss at the Great Plains Action Society
* It is not true that there is only one way to build a channel, and the settler is assumed to be the builder
  * Some channels are built from the other side and offered. Where one exists, the obligation is to use it correctly — unsummarized, at full length, in their own voice — not to build another.
    * [The article Zitkála-Šá wrote](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/10376/pg10376-images.html) about her boarding school experience is an example.
    * As are invitations to work at the Great Plains Action Society’s Urban Resilience Hub
* Because I, of necessity, write from my own experience, there is the implication that Quaker practices are required to make channels. Which wasn’t intended, or true.
  * The initial need to sense that there is something you don’t know can come from any reflective or meditative practice.
  * Or may come from a challenge or a story from someone who holds the knowledge you don’t have
* The knowledge through an established channel flows in **both** directions.
  * Otherwise, it would just be extractive
    * A reminder that you need to contribute to the channel in an ongoing manner

A better statement would be:

> Non-Native people cannot respond well to what Native people endured, and still suffer, until they understand it — and understanding of that kind arrives only through a channel: a relationship with the people who hold that knowledge, built over years, entered by invitation, and carrying in both directions.

Or a shorter form:

> *Understanding that leads to response arrives only through a channel — a relationship with the people who hold the knowledge, built over years, entered by invitation, carrying both ways.*

# My Quaker meeting and channels

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-26* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/26/my-quaker-meeting-and-channels/)[^original-post]

This concept of channels into knowledge is causing tensions in my Quaker meeting. Which is ironic, because a few members of my meeting have spent about thirty years building relationships with Native people in the vicinity. They have deep relationships of trust with those working on the annual Prairie Awakening/Prairie Awoke celebration, held just a few miles from our meetinghouse.

The meeting has supported those Friends in their work. But the meeting has not built on the channel they developed — and it could not have. **Channels are relationships between individuals.** That is their nature, and it is the whole difficulty. Friends who have not been involved in building those relationships do not have that channel themselves. It cannot be inherited, and it cannot be held on the meeting’s behalf.

What the existing channel offers is an opportunity — a door other Friends could walk through to begin building their own. The meeting has donated money when that was requested, and many members have attended the annual celebration. The goal would be more channels, as more Friends become directly involved with this Native community. But each Friend would have to build their own, however parallel it runs to someone else’s.

I had hoped thirty years of that work with Prairie Awakening would make it easier for Friends to begin building similar channels with the Great Plains Action Society. But, Friends will not have a channel to GPAS until they do their own work with the people of GPAS — not with GPAS as an organization, but with the people.

## What a decade looks like

My relationship with Sikowis Nobiss, founder and Executive Director of GPAS, began nearly a decade ago. We walked together on the First Nation-Farmer Climate Unity March in 2018, which was designed to create the conditions to begin building channels among us. Since then we have worked together many times — at pipeline protests, at actions about racist mascots and monuments.

I’ve been excited about how the GPAS Indigenous-led Urban Resilience and Innovation Hub has come into being. A concrete example of so many ideas put into practice.

When Sikowis asked for volunteers to come to the Hub to help remodel the buildings, and to cut down trees so we could fence the urban farm, I encouraged members of my meeting to participate. **A fundamental part of decolonial work is following Indigenous leadership, and that request was an opportunity to do it.** I was clearly led to go, and I have been to every work-week held there.

My meeting has a very small number of active members. One of them, Jon, has come to a couple of the work-weeks with me, which is great. He has begun creating his own relationships — his own channels — with people at the Hub.

## The problem

It must be confusing to members of my meeting that I am now asking them not to simply drop in at the Hub. I appreciate their interest, and I asked for it. I encouraged them to come when there were work-weeks. I have been writing and speaking about this at meeting a great deal.

Some of them want to see for themselves what I’ve been describing. That is how Friends have traditionally engaged with justice work — by visiting the organizations doing it. **It is the only model most of us were ever given.** It is also the wrong one here, for two reasons.

The first is Indigenous leadership. Jon and I went to work-weeks *organized by the Hub*. An invitation came from the Hub, asking for volunteers for specific projects. Those were the times I let Friends know about and encouraged to attend.

Those hours of shared, difficult manual labor quickly built bonds among those of us who did attend . Channels being built.

The second is that the situation has changed. The work we did has brought the Hub far enough along that its work in the community has begun — work driven by the Indigenous leadership of the Hub. GPAS has very few staff, and they are fully engaged in that work while still building the place. Interest in the Hub is appreciated. Unannounced arrivals interrupt the work.

**Expecting to be welcomed to visit, unannounced, is a colonial practice.** I don’t say that to accuse anyone in my meeting. I say it because it is the habit we inherited and will keep repeating until we notice it. The Hub is a sacred space, and we should act accordingly.

## What I am proposing

I’ve spoken with Sikowis about Friends who are interested in visiting the Hub doing some preparation beforehand, and she supports the idea.

My hope is that my meeting will be willing to develop that preparation — and to build it as a model other people considering a visit to the Hub could use. That would turn our confusion into something useful to the Hub rather than something it has to manage. It would also be the clearest demonstration I know of how a channel is actually built.

In the meantime, Friends can be connected to the work of the Hub by means of the Decolonial Repair Network (DRN), that was formed specifically for the purpose of teaching non-Native people about the impacts of colonization on Indigenous communities, and to share about the work of the Hub. We meet the first Wednesday of every month at 7:00 pm Central time. You can sign up to attend these Zoom meetings here: <https://www.honornativelandfund.org/decolonialrepairnetwork>

The root of my struggles was trying to figure out what I should do. My Quaker community included nearly twenty men who refused to cooperate with the Selective Service System — men I respected a great deal, because they understood the consequences of their decisions and choose to risk suffering for them. Many served time in prison.

The most difficult part of all of this wasn’t making the decision to refuse to cooperate with the draft. It was how to deal with how upset my family was that I was risking a felony conviction that would affect the rest of my life.

But it was very clear to me that this decision would determine the course of the rest of my life where my spirituality was concerned. **I knew that if I compromised by not taking those risks, I would have no spiritual integrity.**

I wonder what young people, including young Friends, are thinking about their lives today. Thinking about it in terms of leadings.

It came to me — that is, *I felt led* — to use what I wrote in my journal during those turbulent times to show some of what I was going through. And to include what that looks like some fifty years later.
