*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-08-30* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/08/30/leadings-continued/)[^original-post]

![](https://i0.wp.com/channelsintoknowledge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-31.png)

Yesterday I wrote:

> It came to me — that is, *I felt led* — to use what I wrote in my journal during those turbulent times to show some of what I was going through

I wondered if you might think that I was trivializing what a leading is. Do I consider any decision I make a leading? No, I do not.

Each morning I sit quietly, trying to discern what I should write about that day. It is definitely a spiritual practice. Even though I usually have a general idea, a long range plan, I usually don’t know specifically what I will write that day. The most difficulty I have is waiting to hear what I should write. Until then, there is some tension. Once I know what to write about, the writing comes pretty easily. Although it routinely takes about four hours to complete each day.

Sometimes I don’t have a clear picture of what to write. Sometimes I try to force it, and that rarely goes well.

It is surprising that I do get an answer almost every day. This is sometimes referred to as ***expectant waiting***. That concept also applies to what people who come to Quaker meeting try to do, as a group.

And points out something about leadings. You **can create** the conditions that make it more likely to “hear” a spiritual message, or a leading. A quiet space is important. Not that a leading can’t occur in the middle of noise or chaos because that can happen.

Practice over time can make it easier to come into the silence and be attentive to what the Spirit might be saying, what leading might appear.

So when I wrote “I felt led’, I didn’t mean “I decided to…” I meant that I had discerned what to write about. Discern means to recognize or perceive something.

![](https://i0.wp.com/channelsintoknowledge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-32.png)

Four clauses about leadings, and each rules something out.

* *Arrives rather than being reasoned to* rules out the good idea.
* *Something you had no way of knowing you wanted* rules out the preference.
* *Requiring something you would not have chosen* rules out the convenient.
* *Persisting until it is obeyed or refused* rules out the passing impulse.

“People like… us”. People who are open to leadings that brought them to the Hub, which is considered a sacred space. People who joyfully put in the time and energy to build what we are led to do.

# The draft and youth today

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-09-01* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/09/01/the-draft-and-youth-today/)[^original-post]

## A break in a relationship?

What does the idea of ***channels into knowledge*** mean in the context of young people today and the draft? I think it points to a problem we have right now with our Quaker history against war, and with what young Friends may not be learning about it.

Legislation for ***automatic registration with the Selective Service System*** for males aged 18-25 was included in the **Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA)** and will go into effect December 18, 2026. (See details below).

## Three kinds of not-knowing

There are three kinds of not-knowing:

* Missing
* Withheld
* Abandoned

---

I’ve been writing about this in the context of Quakers and our relationships with Native peoples. In particular, related to the Quaker involvement in the Indian boarding schools, and taking land. That relates to knowledge that was ***WITHHELD***.

The question here, related to what young Friends may or may not know about the draft is, ***is this a gap in the information, or a break in a relationship?***

The answer varies, as some Quaker meetings and the Friends Committee on National Legislation (FCNL) have been generating knowledge about the changes in the draft registration law. These things can help fill in knowledge that is ***MISSING***.

My sense is that in the years since the draft was employed in the Vietnam War era, this information has been ***ABANDONED***. The information was kept, but hasn’t been opened since.

Those of us who lived through the draft era of the 1960s have an obligation to offer this knowledge to young people facing a similar problem today. That might have to begin by making them aware of the new legislation at all, since one effect of automatic registration is that a young person can be registered without ever being told.

During the Vietnam War era, refusing to cooperate with the Selective Service System was one way a young person could object to that system. Taking that possibility away from young people today silences a way of refusing to be complicit in the machinery of war. It removes a way of taking a moral stand.

## Build a Channel

I think there is a widespread problem in the relationships between older Friends and younger Friends. This is an opportunity — and I feel it as an obligation — to rebuild those relationships. In previous times of conflict there were **channels** between older and younger Friends. The communities were more tightly knit, and the youth were in contact with their elders. Many young Friends attended their Quaker meetings.

Do those channels exist today? Where they do not, we should build them, or re-open them.

## What does ***WITHHELD*** mean here?

My contention, related to Quakers and Native peoples, is that information was ***WITHHELD***. Nothing else explains the damning silence of the history of the Indian boarding schools. Or our continued occupation of Native land.

Do we also have a situation where the knowledge about Quakers and the draft was essentially ***WITHHELD*** from our youth? The answer will vary from Quaker meeting to meeting. Those who are engaged with their youth regarding the draft and conscientious objection are not withholding knowledge.

Understand, **withheld** in this case ***does not mean*** that we actively kept this knowledge away from youth. It is what happens when the relationship between adult Quakers and youth breaks down. Which has much wider implications. We see this in the dwindling membership of many Quaker meetings today, as the elders die, and few youth join.

This is an opportunity, and I believe an obligation, to strengthen or to create the relationships at each end of a channel into this knowledge — knowledge adult Quakers have, and young people need.

## What now?

In what new ways can we older Quakers engage with young people now? Discussions and actions related to this legislation is one opening for that to happen.

---

![](https://i0.wp.com/channelsintoknowledge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/image.png)

---

## Automatic registration with the Selective Service System

The mandate for automatic registration with the Selective Service System (referred to as the ***draft***) was enacted as part of the **Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA)**, which was passed by Congress and signed into law in **December 2025**.

Section 535 of the FY 2026 NDAA formally amends the Military Selective Service Act. It removes the legal requirement for individual young men (ages 18–25) to manually register themselves and replaces it with a statutory requirement for the Selective Service System (SSS) to register them automatically using data pulled from other federal and state databases (such as Social Security records, the DMV, and the Census Bureau).

The automated system applies to draft-eligible males between ages 18 and 25 (including U.S. citizens and non-citizen residents such as green card holders and refugees). Registration was not expanded to include women.

The official start date for automatic enrollment as **December 18, 2026**

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-09-21* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/09/21/quakers-and-the-macklemore-sheeran-controversy/)[^original-post]

I was surprised when I realized this current controversy surrounding musician and activist Macklemore being forced out of Ed Sheeran’s concert tour provides another way of looking at Quakers’ history since settling on this land.

Macklemore has been an outspoken critic of the Israeli-American genocide occurring in Gaza and the West Bank for years. He shouted “Free Palestine” performing “Hind’s Hall” at the September 5 MetLife show, and Patriots owner Robert Kraft pushed venues to bar him over it.

## Ed Sheeran

Ed Sheeran said the decision to remove Macklemore was not made by him (Sheeran). That he has always tried to maintain his political neutrality.

> I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed
>

# Stolen land

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-09-23* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/09/23/stolen-land/)[^original-post]

One helpful response to the last post was an objection to using the term “stolen land.” How could land be stolen from a people who don’t believe in land ownership?

That way of looking at it shows what was stolen were the “commons”, the land and water that supported and were cared for by the whole community. The Statute of Merton in 1235 gave lords of the manor in England the right to enclose parts of the common “waste,” as long as they left enough pasture for their tenants. The largest wave of enclosures occurred between about 1750 to 1850 was referred to as Parliamentary enclosure, when Parliament passed thousands of individual enclosure acts, essentially leaving no commons.

This meant that increasing numbers of the people in England no longer had access to land for shelter and to grow their own food. The main driver of immigration from England to this country was this economic desperation. The immigrants wanted to have their own land, and brought that concept with them to this country.

Many ways were used to dispossess Native people of their land.

The Dawes Act of 1887 was used to take Native land by creating parcels of land, leaving some to the Native people, and selling the “excess”. Thus the idea of private property.

In 1980, in *United States v. Sioux Nation*, the Supreme Court ruled that the Black Hills had been taken illegally. The Lakota have refused the money ever since, because they want the land, not payment. So “stolen” isn’t an Old World idea projected onto Native people. It’s the US government’s own judgment of its own conduct.

Every treaty the United States entered into with Native people was broken, which I thought meant that the property transfers in those treaties were no longer valid. That the land returned to the Native people. However, when the Kiowa and Comanche challenged the federal government’s unilateral breakup of their reservation as a blatant violation of the 1867 Medicine Lodge Treaty, the Supreme Court ruled that Congress has **“plenary power”** (absolute authority) over Indian affairs. The Court decided that Congress has the constitutional authority to unilaterally break treaties with Indian tribes at will, and the courts cannot invalidate congressional acts for doing so. Plenary Power and Treaty Abrogation (*Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock*, 1903).

Indigenous peoples use the phrase “stolen land”. A fundamental concept in justice work is to respect the terminology and language used by those who are oppressed.

There is a misconception that these discussions about Land Back and property are about returning all the land in this country to Native people. That is not the case. It is about centering Native voices in guiding how the land and water are repaired and treated now.

That does not mean non-Native people would have no power. It means that the power will be returned to us, all the people, to be shared.

Besides being the right thing to do, we desperately need Indigenous help in repairing and restoring our environment and ourselves. Its about hope.

There are a rapidly growing number of instances of returning land to Indigenous peoples and ways. I’ve been writing here about my work with the Great Plains Action Society’s Indigenous-led Urban Resilience Hub in Iowa City, Iowa. All of this on one acre of land downtown. This is a model that your community can adapt to help you prepare for disruption.
(See: <https://www.honornativelandfund.org/decolonialrepairnetwork> )

# Recalibrate

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-09-28* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/09/28/recalibrate/)[^original-post]

Hope isn’t a word I hear much these days. But I am hopeful about some things. During times of stress communities come together, as they always have. New and stronger relationships are built that extend beyond the moment.

It’s frightening to think about all of the changes that have occurred in recent years. And to witness the increasingly negative consequences of many of those changes that we are seeing now. It is no longer possible to deny the devastation of our environment and its global consequences.

Now, there are three things happening at once:

* The systems people depend on are failing.
* The tools we once used to repair those systems no longer work.
* Quiet but rapidly growing grassroots movements are forming, as local people come together to meet their community’s needs because the government can’t or won’t.

If you haven’t been fortunate enough to be directly involved in such grassroots communities, you’ve likely heard stories in the media or by word of mouth. These are the stories that give us hope, for ourselves and our communities.

To have hope you need to believe positive change can happen. Without hope, the change you want isn’t likely to occur. Hope is the driving force when obstacles appear. For many, hope comes from our faith.

## Vision

To have hope you need a vision you are working towards. We all have only so much time and energy and the demands on both seem ever increasing. We have to protect ourselves and our resources. And we must also love our neighbors.

Quakers have a long history of building communities. Many of those tools and experiences are greatly needed now by the wider society in this country. Giving others hope is one of the most important things we can do at this time.

## Recalibrate

None of us can know what it is that we don’t know until we have an experience or teacher that shows us that. I’m trying to share what I’ve learned.

But the point of this blog is there is some knowledge that can only be learned by direct experience.

That means face to face presence in oppressed communities. Repeatedly. Trust must be built, and that can take a long time. But will only happen by repeatedly showing up.

Recalibrate is the word that comes to me now. We are moving ever more deeply and rapidly into conditions of great change. This is a chance to recalibrate how we do justice work. A chance to change how we work for change.

* Can we radically practice the belief that there is that of God or the Spirit in every single child, woman and man?
* Can we wait expectantly for what might come from those who aren’t Quakers?
* Can we help center the voices of Black, Indigenous and other people of color?
* Can we avoid judging how messages are delivered?
* Can we listen for new language?
* Can we be like a child and absorb everything around us when we enter new spaces? This is our new school. Engage all of your senses.
* It’s a school where we learn by watching and being present. We should avoid adding to the burden of those who are oppressed by asking them to teach us. It is traumatizing to revisit these memories.
* Will we attend local gatherings of different communities and cultures?
* Building relationships requires many meetings and experiences together over extended time.
* Can we refrain from offering any suggestions until we have spent significant time with a given group?
* Can we be sensitive to the trauma communities and individuals have suffered, even before we understand what those traumas are and how they occurred?
* This is spiritually demanding work.
* This is spiritually rewarding work.
* This is the practical work of hope.

---

## Next step

There are a growing number of people and groups coming together to do this work. The one I’m involved with is the [Decolonial Repair Network (DRN)](https://www.honornativelandfund.org/decolonialrepairnetwork). The DRN was established over two years ago for the purpose of helping with recalibration as discussed in this post. In this case, supporting the Great Plains Action Society’s work. It has become increasingly clear that we are reaching a precipice. Too many things have been broken. Quakers have long had a strong voice in Washington politics in the Friends Committee on National Legislation (FCNL). But such voices are now increasingly drowned out by the flood of money in politics. We are at a precipice because the tools we could once use to repair the damage no longer work. We can’t turn back. More fundamentally, the injustices of this country’s settling have never been addressed. The consequences will continue to reverberate, impacting us all, until they are dealt with in a just manner. Oppressed communities have long demanded justice, and are being heard more widely

There are increasing opportunities for justice work. And increasing risk, in some cases, from policing and authoritarianism.

Many more of us are joining the millions in this country who are already in survival mode as capitalism continues to fail.

As an overview, these are seven systems whose failures will keep driving change, and some alternatives that are being built. My experiences include Des Moines Mutual Aid’s food giveaway, and the Great Plains Action Society’s work.

Which of these systems is failing where you live, and who nearby is already building something in its place?

| Law and politics | Gridlock; courts that no longer check power | Neighborhood assemblies; local officials pressed to lease or transfer public land |

| Spirit | Isolation, despair, spiritual poverty | Regular shared meals and silence; elders and young people working side by side |

# Practicing Hope

*Channels Into Knowledge, 2026-10-03* · [Original post](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/10/03/practicing-hope/)[^original-post]

[**Being on a precipice**](https://channelsintoknowledge.com/2026/10/02/on-the-precipice/), as I wrote yesterday, implies great change is about to happen abruptly.

I’ve been dwelling on all the systems that are breaking or broken. On the destruction, injustices and pain that are building to the breaking point, the edge of the precipice.

But the other half of the precipice story is that once you pass the tipping point, those prior conditions are no longer relevant. They are left behind. Eventually. Some of those conditions losing their relevance much faster than others. It’s definitely not the case that suddenly you don’t have to be concerned about what led to the break. Some of those things hang on for some time.

Those of us working for justice can recognize this as a tipping point, and do what we can to move past the precipice. Onward toward peace.

At my Quaker meeting last week we had a great discussion about what gives us hope today.

We have to find ways to hold onto hope, our own and others’.

Did you know that hope is something you can actually practice and get better at? I hadn’t realized that until I read [**this sermon by Quinn Norton**](https://www.emptywheel.net/2018/04/30/it-is-bitter-tea-that-involves-you-so-a-sermon-on-hope/). Since then, I’ve often signed my email messages “***practicing hope***“. I realized that was something I had practiced without being aware I was doing so. Since then, I’ve been paying more attention, practicing more. This helped me finally understand why so many people resolutely refuse to look at injustice. They haven’t learned to practice hope, yet.
